abstract: Motivation: Genetic diseases are complex phenomena that are currently defined by their clinical symptoms, rather than by the combinations of variants that give rise to them. Incomplete penetrance and phenotypic variability indicate that the genomic background contributes to the effect of variants. Recent advancements in genomics have produced vast amounts of data and created new opportunities to study genetic diversity across human populations. Much of this variation is inherited as recombination-defined contiguous segments, called haploblocks. We previously introduced a novel methodology for genomic hash encoding, the Genomic Cluster Engine, which groups individuals into clusters using phased haploblock sequences. By encoding each haploblock sequence as a compact hash, the characterization of genomic backgrounds, the subtyping of etiologies and the inference of local ancestry become fast and scalable. Results: We have optimized the Genomic Cluster Engine pipeline for large genomic datasets through parallelization and improved memory management. We applied our pipeline to 2,548 individuals across 26 populations from the 1000 Genomes Project and produced a dataset of haploblock-based genomic hashes for the resulting clusters. The genomic hashes and clusters can be used for investigating variant effects in the context of their haplotype backgrounds or for genotype-phenotype association studies. This comprehensive dataset is now publicly available, providing a valuable resource for both academic and industry researchers worldwide. Availability: The haploblock boundaries, sequences, clusters and genomic hashes for the 1000 Genomes Project are available under the CC0 license at https://data.haploblocks.org and on the Registry of Open Data on AWS https://registry.opendata.aws.
